title: Firkas Fortress and the Maritime Museum

where.label: supported
where.says: The Firkas Fortress is on the west side of Chania harbor, built in 1620 to protect the harbor.
quote: on the West side of Chania harbour
In 1620, the Firkas Fortress was built to protect Chania's harbour.

bastion.label: supported
bastion.says: The fortress is close to San Salvatore Bastion, the northwest corner of the walls.
quote: San Salvatore Bastion (also known as Gritti Bastion), on the northwest corner
The Firkas Fortress is located close to San Salvatore Bastion.

layers.label: supported
layers.says: The inner walls were first built in antiquity and rebuilt by the Byzantines; the outer walls were built by Venice in the 16th century; parts of both remain.
quote: The inner city walls were first built in antiquity, and were rebuilt by the Byzantine Empire. The outer walls were built in the 16th century by the Republic of Venice.
parts of both the Byzantine and Venetian walls remain intact

hell.label: estimate
hell.says: By around the 3rd century BC, Cydonia was walled.
quote: By the Hellenistic period, in around the 3rd century BC, the Cydonia was surrounded by walls.

byz.label: supported
byz.says: The Byzantines reinforced the walls in the 6th and 7th centuries AD; Saracens destroyed the city in 828; the Byzantines later built a fortress on Kastelli in the 10th century against another Arab invasion.
quote: These were reinforced by the Byzantine Empire in the 6th and 7th centuries AD, before the city was destroyed by Saracens in 828.
built a new fortress on the hill of Kastelli in the 10th century, to prevent a second Arab invasion

ven-1336.label: supported
ven-1336.says: Venice occupied Crete in the 13th century; in 1336 it decided to wall the suburbs, finished within 20 years.
quote: Crete was occupied by the Republic of Venice in the 13th century.
In 1336, it was decided that walls were to be built around the burgs, and the fortifications were completed within 20 years.

sanmicheli.label: supported
sanmicheli.says: Facing the Ottoman threat in the early 16th century, Venice began new walls in 1536 to a design by Michele Sanmicheli, finished in 1568; with a fortress on Thodorou they cost 87,000 ducats. (wp-chania gives 1538 for the start of the Venetian fortifications.)
quote: By the early 16th century, the expanding Ottoman Empire became a major threat for the Venetians

Work on the new fortifications began in 1536, to a design of Michele Sanmicheli. They were completed in 1568. Construction of the fortifications of Chania as well as a fortress on Thodorou cost a total of 87,000 ducats.
It used to be surrounded by the old Venetian fortifications that started to be built in 1538.

arms.label: supported
arms.says: In 1630 the city had 319 cannons and 30,695 cannonballs.
quote: In 1630, the city was armed with 319 cannons, 30,695 cannonballs

dims.label: supported
dims.says: The walls were up to 20 m (66 ft) high with a ditch 60 m (200 ft) wide and 15 m (49 ft) deep.
quote: The walls were up to 20 m (66 ft) high, and were surrounded by a ditch which was 60 m (200 ft) wide and 15 m (49 ft) deep.

siege.label: supported
siege.says: The Ottoman navy arrived on 23 June 1645, landed 15 miles west, the militia fled; after a 56-day siege the city fell on 22 August when the southwest walls were breached.
quote: The fifth Ottoman–Venetian War broke out when the Ottoman Navy arrived off Crete on 23 June 1645. The Ottomans first landed 15 miles west of Chania, and the local militia fled before them. They besieged the city for 56 days, and it fell on 22 August after the walls on the southwestern part of the city were breached.

persec.label: supported
persec.says: Many Cretans fled persecution; many others were slaughtered or converted to Islam.
quote: Many Cretans fled to escape persecution, many others were slaughtered or converted to Islam.

ottoman.label: supported
ottoman.says: The Ottomans restored and later modernized the walls; Chania stayed under Ottoman control until November 1898.
quote: After the siege, the Ottomans restored the breached walls, and later modernized and renovated them. Chania remained under Ottoman control until November 1898.

demolish.label: supported
demolish.says: The Cretan State demolished parts of the south walls in the early 20th century because they limited the city's growth.
quote: Parts of the walls on the south side were demolished by the Cretan State in the early 20th century, since they limited the growth of the city.

union.label: supported
union.says: On 1 December 1913, at the formal ceremony of union, the Greek flag was raised at the Firka Fortress with Venizelos and King Constantine I present.
quote: On 1 December, the formal ceremony of union took place: the Greek flag was raised at the Firka Fortress in Chania, with Eleftherios Venizelos and King Constantine I in attendance.
The union of the Creten State with Greece was celebrated at Firkas Fortress on 1 December 1913.

capital.label: supported
capital.says: In 1898 the Great Powers made Chania the capital of the semi-autonomous Cretan State, with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner.
quote: In 1898, during the final moves towards independence and enosis—union with Greece—the Great Powers made Chania the capital of the semi-autonomous Cretan State (Kritiki Politeia), with Prince George of Greece, the High Commissioner of Crete living here.

venizelos.label: supported
venizelos.says: Venizelos was a young Athens-trained lawyer from Chania; in March 1905 he and his supporters gathered at Therisos in the hills near Chania.
quote: a young, Athens-trained lawyer from Chania, Eleftherios Venizelos
in March 1905, Venizelos and his supporters gathered in the village of Therisos, in the hills near Chania

pm.label: supported
pm.says: Venizelos's election as prime minister of Greece in 1910 led to union in 1913, after the Balkan Wars.
quote: His later election as the prime minister of Greece (1910) eventually led to Crete's union with Greece on 1 December 1913, following the Balkan Wars.

souda.label: supported
souda.says: The Great Powers tacitly accepted the union by lowering their flags at the Souda fortress on 14 February 1913.
quote: The Great Powers tacitly recognized the fait accompli by the act of lowering their flags from the Souda fortress on 14 February 1913

akrotiri.label: supported
akrotiri.says: In 1897 a Greek flag was raised at the rebel camp at Akrotiri, and Great Power ships bombarded the rebel positions; a shell threw down the flag, which was raised again.
quote: Venizelos spent the night in Akrotiri and a Greek flag was raised.
with the ships of the Great Powers bombarding the rebel positions at Akrotiri. A shell threw down the flag, which was raised up again immediately.
There was that famous day in February 1897

flag-myth.label: legend
flag-myth.says: Venizelos's actions at Akrotiri became a set-piece of his myth; as the story is told, he defied the warships at Souda: 'You have cannon-balls, fire away! But our flag will not come down.'
quote: Venizelos's subsequent actions at Akrotiri form a central set-piece in his myth.
Venizelos turned towards the port of Souda, where the warships were anchored, and explained: "You have cannon-balls – fire away! But our flag will not come down"

museum.label: supported
museum.says: The Maritime Museum of Crete's main collection is at the entrance to the Firka Fortress; it holds ship models, nautical instruments, paintings, photographs and war relics, arranged from the Bronze Age to today.
quote: Its collection includes models of ships, nautical instruments, painting, historical photographs and war relics. The material is classified chronologically, starting from the Bronze Age up to our times.
The main collection is located at the entrance to the Firka Fortress

floor1.label: supported
floor1.says: First floor: ancient ship models, a model of the Venetian fortified town and port, a shipbuilding model with a rowing ship, and a marine life room.
quote: The exhibits of the first floor include models of ancient ships, a model of the fortified town and port under Venetian rule, a model that shows shipbuilding and repair buildings, with a rowing ship inside. There is also a room dedicated to natural marine life with a large collection of sea shells, sea sponges, corals, fossils and fish skin mounts.

floor2.label: supported
floor2.says: Second floor: modern Hellenic Navy models, the full bridge of a destroyer, two torpedo propulsion units, and a section on the German invasion of Crete.
quote: The second floor exhibits include models of modern Hellenic Navy ships, destroyers, a missile boat, a landing ship with trucks and APVs on board. The exhibits include the full bridge of a destroyer and two torpedo propulsion units. A section of the museum is dedicated to the German invasion of Crete.

battle.label: supported
battle.says: On 20 May 1941 German paratroopers landed near Maleme Airfield and Chania; most were engaged by New Zealanders defending the airfield and by Greek forces near Chania.
quote: At 08:00 on 20 May 1941, German paratroopers, jumping out of dozens of Junkers Ju 52 aircraft, landed near Maleme Airfield and the town of Chania.
Most of the parachutists were engaged by New Zealanders defending the airfield and by Greek forces near Chania.

moro.label: supported
moro.says: At the Moro Shipyard, at the east end of the harbor, a smaller exhibition is dominated by a 17 m experimental Minoan ship replica built 2001-2004, later sailed and rowed to Piraeus.
quote: In the Moro Shipyard at the eastern end of the harbour is a smaller exhibition of ancient naval architecture.  This is dominated by a 17m experimental replica Minoan ship constructed between 2001 and 2004 (and eventually sailed and rowed to Piraeus).

trade.label: supported
trade.says: In Late Minoan IIIA and IIIB, Kydonia was a large commercial and maritime center exporting pottery, oil, perfume and wine across the Aegean.
quote: In the LM IIIA and LM IIIB, it was a large commercial and maritime center, exporting pottery, oil, perfume and wine throughout the Aegean.

parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: At the fortress, on the west side of the harbor, looking out over the water.

paras.t: This is the Firkas Fortress, on the west side of Chania's harbor. It was built early in the seventeenth century to protect the harbor, close to the San Salvatore Bastion, the northwest corner of the old city walls.
The stone underfoot can be uneven, and there's little shade up on the walls. Take your time, and carry water.

parts.name: Walls on walls
parts.stand: Turn and look back toward the town.

paras.t: Chania's walls come in layers. The inner walls first went up in antiquity, and the Byzantines rebuilt them. The outer walls are Venetian, from the 1500s. Parts of both still stand.

By around the 3rd century BC, ancient Cydonia had walls. The Byzantines strengthened them in the 500s and 600s, but in 828 Saracens destroyed the city. When the Byzantines came back, they built a new fortress on Kastelli hill in the 900s, to stop a second Arab invasion.
Venice took Crete in the 13th century. In 1336, as the town spilled outside its old walls, Venice decided to wall in the new neighborhoods, and the job was done within 20 years.

Then, in the early 1500s, the Ottoman Empire became the big threat. So in the fifteen-thirties, work began on new walls, designed by Michele Sanmicheli. They were finished in 1568. Together with a fortress at a place called Thodorou, they cost 87,000 ducats.
Picture the scale. The walls stood up to 20 meters high, about 66 feet, with a ditch in front 60 meters wide and 15 deep. In 1630 the city had 319 cannons and 30,695 cannonballs.

parts.name: The siege of 1645
parts.stand: Look out to sea, past the harbor entrance.

paras.t: All that stone didn't save the city. In June 1645 the Ottoman fleet arrived. After a siege of 56 days, the city fell on 22 August, when the walls on the town's southwest side, away from the sea, were breached.
Here's how it began. The Ottoman navy arrived off Crete on 23 June. The troops landed 15 miles west of Chania, and the local militia fled before them.
Many Cretans fled to escape persecution. Many others were slaughtered, or converted to Islam.

The Ottomans repaired the breached walls and later modernized them, and Chania stayed under Ottoman rule until November 1898. Then, early in the twentieth century, parts of the south walls were torn down, because they were holding the growing city back.

parts.name: The flag of 1913
parts.stand: Stay up on the fortress, facing the harbor.

paras.t: This fortress is remembered above all for one day. On 1 December 1913, at the ceremony of Crete's union with Greece, the Greek flag was raised here, with Eleftherios Venizelos and King Constantine the First looking on.

It was a long road. In 1898, Chania became the capital of the semi-autonomous Cretan State, with Prince George of Greece as High Commissioner. A young lawyer from Chania, Eleftherios Venizelos, pushed for union with Greece. In March 1905 he and his supporters gathered at Therisos, in the hills near Chania. In 1910 he was elected prime minister of Greece, and that, after the Balkan Wars, led to union.
And earlier in 1913, in February, the Great Powers lowered their own flags at the Souda fortress, their quiet way of accepting the union in practice.

As the story is told, early in 1897, during a revolt, a Greek flag was raised at the rebel camp at Akrotiri, and the warships of the Great Powers shelled the rebel positions. A shell knocked the flag down, and it went straight back up.
Akrotiri became part of the Venizelos myth. As the story was told, he turned toward the warships at Souda and said: You have cannon-balls, fire away! But our flag will not come down.

parts.name: The Maritime Museum
parts.stand: At the museum, by the entrance to the fortress.

paras.t: Right at the entrance to the fortress is the Maritime Museum of Crete. Ship models, nautical instruments, paintings, old photographs and war relics, all laid out in order, from the Bronze Age to today.

On the museum's first exhibition floor, look for models of ancient ships, and a model of the walled town and port under Venice. It's the easiest way to picture the walls we've been talking about. There's a model of a shipyard with a rowing ship inside, and a whole room of sea life: shells, sponges, corals and fossils.

On the floor above, it's the modern Hellenic Navy: destroyers, a missile boat, a landing ship, even the full bridge of a destroyer, and two torpedo propulsion units. One section is given over to the German invasion of Crete.

That invasion began on the morning of 20 May 1941, when German paratroopers landed near Maleme Airfield and near the town of Chania. Most were met by New Zealanders defending the airfield and by Greek forces near Chania.

parts.name: The Minoan ship
parts.stand: If you have time, walk along the harbor to the Moro Shipyard at its eastern end, and see if it's open.

paras.t: Here at the Moro Shipyard, at the harbor's eastern end, the museum keeps a 17-meter replica of a Minoan ship, built as an experiment between 2001 and 2004, and later sailed and rowed all the way to Piraeus.
It belongs here. In the late Minoan age, the town under old Chania, ancient Kydonia, was a large commercial and maritime center, shipping pottery, oil, perfume and wine all over the Aegean.
Walls, flags and ships. This harbor has seen people defend what they had, and fight for what they hoped for. Before you go, look out at the water, the same water those Minoan rowers knew.
